title: How to Answer Hard Questions About the Faith
excerpt: You do not need every answer. You need honesty, a little courage, and the willingness to say the three words most Christians are afraid to say.
body:
Sooner or later someone you care about will ask you a question you cannot answer well. Why does God allow children to suffer. Why would a good God send anyone to hell. How can you believe an old book over modern science. If your faith depends on never being asked these things, it is not faith. It is avoidance with a Bible on the shelf.

The good news is that you do not have to be a scholar to handle hard questions. You have to be honest, present, and unafraid. Most people are not looking for a knockdown argument. They are looking for whether you will take their question seriously or panic.

## Find the question under the question

People rarely ask abstract questions for abstract reasons. The man who asks why God allows suffering has often buried someone. The woman who asks about hell is often terrified for a brother who walked away. Before you build a case, ask gently what is behind the question. "Is there something specific that makes you ask?" You may find the real need is not an argument at all. It is a wound. An argument aimed at a wound just deepens it.

This does not mean every question is only emotional. Some people genuinely want the intellectual case, and you should respect that and give it your best. But you cannot tell which kind of question you are facing until you ask. So ask.

## Say the three words

The three words are: I don't know. They are the most credible thing you can say, and we are terrified of them because we think they expose the faith as weak. The opposite is true. When you admit the limits of your knowledge, the things you do affirm gain weight, because the person now knows you are not just selling. "I don't know why your sister died young. I have wrestled with that and I don't have a clean answer. Here is what I do hold onto." That is far stronger than a tidy theodicy that papers over the horror.

Peter says to give a reason for the hope in you with gentleness and respect. Notice he says hope, not proof. You are not a defense attorney with a verdict to win. You are a witness describing what you have seen.

## Do the homework on the recurring ones

A handful of questions come up again and again: suffering, science, the reliability of the Scriptures, the exclusivity of Christ, the church's failures. You will face these for the rest of your life. It is worth reading a serious book or two so you can speak about them without flailing. Not so you can win, but so you are not caught empty. Keller wrote helpfully on doubt. There are good and honest thinkers on each of these. Spend an evening a month learning, and over a year you will be steadier than you imagine.

## Concede what is true

When someone says the church has done terrible things, the worst response is to defend the indefensible. Concede it. We have. We burned people, blessed slavery, covered abuse, baptized empires. Self-implication is not weakness in an argument. It is the only honest posture. The person across from you is testing whether you live in reality or in a bubble. Concede the real failures, and your witness to the real Christ becomes believable.

## Stay in the relationship, not the debate

The goal is never to win and watch the person walk away humiliated. A won argument and a lost friend is a bad trade. If the conversation is heating into combat, you can step back: "This matters too much to rush. Can we keep talking about it over time?" That sentence protects the relationship, and the relationship is where any real change happens anyway. People rarely think their way to faith alone in a debate. They think their way there inside a friendship that gives them room.

## Point past yourself

You are not the answer. You are a finger pointing. When you have said what you can and reached the end of your knowledge, it is fine to say so and to keep the door open. The Spirit does the convincing. Your job is to be honest and to stay near. Bell, I have lost arguments and kept friends, and watched those friends come to faith years later through no cleverness of mine. The patience was the apologetic.

## This week

Pick the one hard question you most dread being asked and spend an hour reading something serious and honest about it. Not to memorize a comeback, but so the dread loosens. Then, the next time anyone raises a hard thing, practice the question under the question: ask what makes them ask before you answer. You will be surprised how often the honest answer was never an argument at all.
